result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend inline edits as the main surface with a panel for questions, reason from redlines and lawyer accountability, and suggest having the panel write its results back as inline suggestions. On item 3 each covers only half: A says AI-generated edits should be marked as such (provenance) but never says outright that edits must wait for acceptance, while B says 'never apply changes silently' but doesn't ask for AI-written text to be distinguishable. Both are about equally focused, with short lists of risks or design points and a modest suggestion to test with users. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers commit to inline editing as the main surface, keep a chat panel for open questions, and reason well from redlining, accountability and the cost of copying text across. B also requires AI-written edits to be marked so they can be told apart from counterparty and colleague changes, and it gives a sharper example of the main risk (a dropped 'not' or a changed defined term). A's 'never apply changes silently' covers acceptance but says nothing about provenance. Both are slightly long, B a little more so with its risks section and test plan.
